segments.original: In Japan, the styles and genres that had been popular since the Pacific War (1941-1945) no longer drew audiences. Some studios went bankrupt, while others relied on repeating a successful formula, such as Shochiku with the long-running Tora-san series - the bittersweet, good-humored story of the rough but essentially decent Torajiro Kuruma (charmingly played by Kiyoshi Atsumi). Forty-eight episodes were produced from 1969 to 1995, providing nostalgic, reliable entertainment for the New Year and the summer Obon festivities.

segments.speaker: narrador
segments.original: Critic Peter Rist called King Hu "the least appreciated of the 'great directors' in the history of cinema" and "one of the most original filmmakers of the 1960s". Hu was the master of wuxia, or martial arts, a genre and tradition that dates back in Chinese cinema to the silent films, but that truly took on its modern form after Hu and some of his contemporaries infused it with a new sophistication in the late 1960s.

segments.speaker: narrador
segments.original: Hu took three years to make A Touch of Zen, which is often cited as his masterpiece, in which he fused Chinese history and Buddhist theology with choreographed action and elegant camera movement. He directs with great skill, and the way he uses the camera, with tracking shots and cranes, sometimes reminiscent of Kenji Mizoguchi (1898-1956), is inventive throughout. Working in Taiwan rather than in Hong Kong, where he had made his first wuxia film, Da zui xia (Come Drink with Me, 1966), he makes the most of the dazzling mountain landscapes, which provide a dramatic backdrop.

segments.speaker: narrador
segments.original: The action scenes are certainly memorable, but the film is notable for its slow build-up, with the first third consisting of hints and foreshadowing rather than explicit violence. There is also a dose of understated humor. Unfortunately, the time and care Hu lavished on the film were not rewarded with immediate commercial success. Its length led to it being shown in two parts in Taiwan and cut by distributors in Hong Kong. In 1975, this final version won a special technical prize at Cannes and, in 2005, A Touch of Zen was ranked ninth on the Hong Kong Film Awards' list of the Best 100 Chinese Motion Pictures.

segments.original: Among the most famous martial arts stars in the West was Bruce Lee (1940-1973), whose incredible fighting skill and early death turned him into a legend. But it was the films directed by Chia-Liang Liu (b. 1936) that elevated the kung fu genre. Films such as Shao Lin San Shi Liu Fang (The 36th Chamber of Shaolin, 1978) fused action, humor and drama. Equally notable are the swordplay films of King Hu (1931-1997), who released his masterpiece Hsia nu (A Touch of Zen, 1971) in 1971, followed by Ying chun ge zhi Fengbo (The Fate of Lee Khan, 1973) in 1973.

segments.original: During the early '70s, wuxia (wuxia novels, usually translated as "martial chivalry") gave way to a new revival of the kung fu film, more graphic, more fearless and spoken in Mandarin, which became the dominant genre throughout the decade until the early '80s. segments.text: Learn more: The Bruce Lee Classic.

segments.speaker: narrador
segments.original: Having established his credentials as an action-movie superstar with low-budget Hong Kong productions such as Fist of Fury and The Big Boss, Bruce Lee, a cha-cha champion (as well as a karate and kung fu champion), only got the chance to complete one film made to Hollywood production standards. Lee, a martial artist whose physical skills reached a spiritual level, invades (along with his allies John Saxon and Jim Kelly) the island lair of a master villain and disposes of hordes of second-tier henchmen (including Jackie Chan, who gets his neck broken in a quick scene).

segments.original: Chang's only rival as the genre's most influential filmmaker was his longtime action choreographer, Lau Kar Leung (1934-2013). Lau began directing his own films for Shaw Brothers in 1975 with Shen da (The Spiritual Boxer, 1975), a forerunner of the kung fu comedy. In subsequent films such as Hung Hsi Kuan (Executioners from Shaolin, 1977), The 36th Chamber of Shaolin (1978) and Shi ba ban wu yi (Legendary Weapons of China, 1982), Lau emphasized the tradition and philosophy of the martial arts and sought to give the fights more authenticity, speed and complexity.

segments.speaker: narrador
segments.original: The kung fu boom was driven in part by enormous international popularity, not only in East Asia. In the West, imported kung fu films, dubbed and often altered and retitled, shown as "B movies" in urban theaters and on television, made Hong Kong cinema widely known - though not necessarily highly respected - for the first time. In particular, African Americans and other ethnic minorities embraced the genre (as exemplified by the popular hip-hop group Wu-Tang Clan), perhaps because it was an almost unprecedented source of adventure stories with non-white heroes, which also revealed a strong current of ethnic and/or nationalist pride.

segments.original: Amid all this, no other figure was more responsible for this international fame than Bruce Lee, a martial artist and actor born in the United States and raised in Hong Kong. Lee completed only four films before his death at age 32: Tang Shan da Xiong (The Big Boss, 1971), Jing Wu Men (Fist of Fury, 1972), Meng Long Guo Jiang (The Way of the Dragon, 1972) and Enter the Dragon (1973). But in this brief career, he became the first global Chinese movie star.

segments.speaker: narrador
segments.original: Asian film historian Patrick Macias attributes his success to "(bringing) the warrior spirit into the present… developing his own fighting style… and possessing superhuman charisma." His first three films broke local box-office records and were successful in much of the world. The English-language film Enter the Dragon, the first coproduction between the United States and Hong Kong, made 90 million dollars worldwide, becoming the most internationally successful film from that part of the globe up to that time. In addition, his decision from the outset to work for the then-new Golden Harvest studio, instead of accepting the Shaws studio's usual, notoriously ungenerous contract, was a factor that contributed to the meteoric rise of Golden Harvest and the decline of Shaw.

segments.original: Following Lee's untimely death, a small industry of fake Lee films emerged, with leads who adopted similar names (Bruce Li, Bruce Lai, etc.), or unused footage of Lee, or some combination of both. But despite this posthumous treatment, Lee continues to cast a long shadow over Hong Kong cinema.

segments.original: The only Chinese actor to rival Lee's global fame is Jackie Chan (b. 1954). Like many kung fu actors of his era, Chan trained in Peking Opera and got his start in film as a stuntman, notably in some of Lee's films. For a while, he was groomed by Lo Wei, director of The Big Boss and Fist of Fury, to be another Bruce Lee "clone" in several films, including Xin Jing Wu Men (New Fist of Fury, 1976), with little success.
